prize_parts.citation: for showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting change international trade, so that reallocation of activity across firms creates gains from trade beyond those arising across industries

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B034 with Helpman and Melitz as a two-person credit. My reasons have been tested against the exchange, and I have narrowed the claim. The contribution is a change in the unit of analysis. Before Melitz (2003), trade models were built on representative firms and gave gains from trade mainly through specialisation across industries. After it, selection into exporting, exporter premia and reallocation within industries became standard channels in trade, productivity measurement and macroeconomics. More than twenty years of firm-level testing in many countries means the maturity test is met without qualification. Credit has a clear core: Melitz supplies the model, and Helpman supplies the lineage through monopolistic-competition trade and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple analysis of exporting versus FDI. In response to the chair's question, the citation should state two things explicitly. First, the discovery is a mechanism, selection and reallocation across firms. Second, it is not a verdict on the size of welfare gains, which depend on model structure. That wording separates the work from the 2008 prize on scale and variety. It also keeps the empirical precursors (Bernard, Jensen and others) and the Eaton-Kortum line outside the claim, because the model organised those facts rather than discovering them. I also concede a point in round 2. B036 has the tighter attribution of the two, and the chair's record shows the laureate set is identical across its supporters. Credit structure is a real criterion, and B034 does not dominate on it. B034 still seems to me the cleaner discovery on maturity and on freedom from disputes over magnitudes. I am not relying on opening counts, which are not evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains thematic and attributional. The 2008 prize recognised new trade theory, and the Committee may judge heterogeneous-firm selection to be a refinement within monopolistic-competition trade, as Friberg argues. Priority is unresolved from the evidence supplied. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related empirical and quantitative contributions, and Yeaple belongs to the Helpman-Melitz strand, so a two-name credit leaves out people with real claims. Welfare conclusions are structure-dependent, and Redding's omission may be criticised. Finally, B036 has a clearer three-person attribution and a decade of replication, and I should not treat my preference as settling the comparison.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B034 with Melitz and Helpman, leaves Redding out, and calls the priority concern involving Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum his most serious reservation. He would credit Melitz with the tractable general-equilibrium integration, not with the exporter facts.
responses.response: I agree with crediting Melitz for the integration and not the facts, and I will use it as the drafting principle for the citation. I would go a step further than I did in round 1. Because the priority question cannot be settled from the evidence here, the citation should name the mechanism, selection and reallocation across firms, and say nothing about who first documented exporter premia. I also accept that this does not remove the reservation. If the Committee judged that the Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum contributions weigh as much as the model, a two-name credit would be hard to defend. That is the finding that would most weaken my position.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B034 second, but says he is less comfortable with the 2008 overlap because the Melitz model sits inside the monopolistic-competition framework Krugman was recognised for, and priority questions remain. He says he would not oppose B034 on scientific grounds.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, but I read the relation differently. Melitz keeps the monopolistic-competition structure and changes what is chosen and what disciplines it. Firms differ, only some export, and the exit and reallocation of low-productivity firms becomes a new source of welfare change. That is testable on firm-level data in a way the earlier representative-firm models were not. It is a mechanism with its own empirical content, not a relabelling. I accept that a Committee member could see it as a refinement. I cannot rule that reading out, and I record it as a real uncertainty.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. She argues the work pairs an explanatory framework with credible quasi-experimental evidence, that the central finding of persistent local adjustment costs has survived stress-testing, and that colleagues persuaded her Dorn should replace Katz.
responses.response: I accept the Dorn-over-Katz reasoning and I find the attribution case for the trio persuasive. I also find the persistence result plausible. My own work on regional development finds that regional adjustment can be slow and path-dependent over very long periods. I would still separate the finding from its magnitude. What I called a mixed record in round 1 was a statement about exposure measures and the role of automation, not about the sign of the local effects. I therefore hold B036 as my first alternative and would not oppose it. My preference for B034 rests on the criteria of maturity and a mechanism not tied to a contested elasticity. It is not a claim that B036 fails on merit.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B036 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn and lists B034 as an alternative. He says B034 may be the stronger and cleaner discovery if the labour entry stalls over attribution, and he discloses that his heterogeneous-firm work is adjacent to B034.
responses.response: I note his disclosure, and it shapes how I read his comments on B034. I treat his alternative ranking as information about his weighing of the fields, not as extra support for the entry. His point that B034 would be the fallback if attribution on B036 stalls is useful, but the chair's record suggests attribution on B036 is largely settled among its supporters. The remaining weaknesses on B036 are the long-run magnitude and the scope of the citation. If those are resolved by a narrow citation worded around exposure and adjustment, as Boppart himself proposes, the practical gap between our positions is smaller than the preference lists suggest.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats heterogeneous-firm selection as a distinct discovery or as a refinement of the new trade theory recognised in 2008.
How to weigh Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and Yeaple, who are outside the two credited names, if priority is judged to be shared.
Whether leaving out Redding is right. I judge his quantitative work to be later and a separate achievement, but colleagues may reasonably reverse that.
How far the wording of a B034 citation can speak to welfare gains given structure-dependence.
Whether the persistence and shift-share debate on B036 matters more than I judge it to, or less. I cannot resolve that from the supplied evidence.
I rely on the round-1 files and my own reading of the literature, without independent verification of credit attributions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Helpman and Melitz, nor for the alternatives. My co-authors and institutional ties are in economic history and political science, and my Lund ties to committee colleagues do not concern these candidates. I disclose that my research on regional growth and adjustment is adjacent to the local-labour-market literature in B036, and that I have no tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson. I also note Boppart's disclosed work on heterogeneous firms and Friberg's disclosed adjacency to B034. These are disclosures, not adjudications. I presented the 2023 prize and the 2025 prize announcement. I treat these as context and not as a preference.
